#4840. The 8 Best Home Office Chairs, Approved by Spine Specialists

The best seats for boosting productivity and evading back pain.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

If you work from home, you know how much of a difference the right office chair can make. Take it from someone who's spent five years working remotely and learned the hard way that the couch isn't the best place to spend a workday. Between a standing desk, an under-desk treadmill, and monitors, outfitting your home office can get expensive. But if you're going to splurge on one piece of WFH gear, an ergonomic office chair that supports your back throughout the workday is a good place to start.

“A supportive chair can reduce the risk of lower back pain, neck and upper back pain, poor circulation, and fatigue,” says Kevin Lees, director of chiropractic operations at The Joint Chiropractic. “This may also lead to improved productivity, enabling individuals to stay focused on their tasks without distractions from trying to get comfortable.”

To find the best home office chairs, our team consulted spine specialists and tested several popular ergonomic chairs for weeks in our own workspaces, sitting for up to eight hours a day. Our favorite is the Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro, which impressed us with its customizable support and easy assembly at a reasonable price compared to premium models from Herman Miller and Steelcase.

The right home office chair will be different for everyone, but there are a lot of factors that will remain the same, like adjustable lumbar support and thick seat cushioning. Keep reading to find which of these eight expert-recommended chairs are the perfect addition to your workday.

Meet the experts: Kevin Lees, Director of Chiropractic Operations at The Joint Chiropractic.Dr. Gbolohan Okubadejo, a spine surgeon and the head of The Institute of Comprehensive Spine Care.

The Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro is our pick for the best home office chair because of its combination of comfort, adjustability, and value. At $499, it’s packed with easy-to-use adjustments that make it a steal. You can customize the seat depth, lumbar support, tilt tension, recline, and more without having to take your eyes away from your work.

After testing the chair for over a month and sitting for four to six hours per workday, WH Digital Designer Taryn Colbert gave it a five out of five, praising how easy it was to assemble and customize. In fact, she found herself using it even when she wasn't working.

“While I work, I sit it up to work on my posture,” she says. When doing her hair or playing computer games, she reclines the chair into what she calls “lounge mode.”

The armrests alone offer five types of adjustment, and you can add a headrest or a taller cylinder for an additional cost. While the mesh version has a low-key look, the leather and vegan leather options are worth considering if you want a bit more style.

Colbert’s biggest gripe was the wide wheelbase, which made it difficult to maneuver through doorways and across carpet.

Still, if you’re looking for a classic ergonomic office chair, this model is great for both first-timers and seasoned remote workers. Its customizable design is intuitive enough to use every day without requiring a four-figure investment.

From the iconic Eames Lounge Chair to the ergonomic Aeron office chair, Herman Miller has earned its reputation for making some of the best seats around. At upwards of $1,500, the Aeron is certainly an investment, but you can customize practically everything, from the arm pads to the casters. It’s available in three sizes, with several options for armrest adjustability, back support, and tilt.

WH Deputy Editor Eunice Lucero-Lee tested the medium-size Aeron in the Jasper colorway for two to four weeks, sitting for six to eight hours per workday. Lucero-Lee, who regularly experiences lower back pain, gave the chair a 5 out of 5.

“This had perfect lumbar support for a whole eight-hour day's work,” she says. She also appreciated the adjustable armrests and how smoothly and quietly the wheels rolled while still offering enough traction and control. (The deep forest green colorway was another bonus.)

Instead of a traditional foam cushion, the Aeron features a breathable mesh seat that offers an almost weightless feeling. And the chair arrives fully assembled—as we'd expect at this price point.

While the steep price tag was Lucero-Lee’s biggest gripe, the Aeron’s customizable fit and excellent lumbar support make it a worthwhile splurge if you spend the better part of your day at your desk.

If you like to lean back and stretch your legs between meetings, the FlexiSpot ErgoX is worth checking out. Beyond customizable lumbar support, seat depth, and armrests, it features an adjustable headrest and a retractable footrest, so you can kick back and put your feet up while catching up on emails or taking a breather between calls.

WH Fitness Reviews Editor Natascha Grief, who already owns a Herman Miller office chair, tested the ErgoX for over a month, sitting for six to eight hours per workday. While she initially found the back support a little uncomfortable, it took about a week for her to get used to sitting in a more upright position.

“I think a good comparison would be switching to a pair of very supportive/corrective shoes after wearing pairs that are less structured,” she says. Once she adjusted to the chair, she liked the firm back support and how the headrest helped her maintain a comfortable neck position.

Grief also loved how comfortable the chair was when fully reclined, though she found the mechanism for pulling out the footrest a little clunky. She ultimately gave the chair a 4 out of 5.

Considering how many adjustments and extras you're getting for the price, the ErgoX is a great option if you prefer a more supportive seat but still want the flexibility to kick back throughout the workday.

Like the Herman Miller Aeron, the Steelcase Gesture comes at a luxury price point, but its sturdy construction, supportive cushioning, and impressive range of adjustments help justify the investment. The chair comes in different materials and colors. Plus you can customize wheels for hard floors or carpet.

Of its many adjustable features, including recline and lumbar support, the most unique is its 360-degree armrests, which allow you to comfortably position your arms whether you're typing on your laptop or scrolling through your phone.

After testing the Gesture for two to four weeks and sitting for two to four hours per workday, WH Managing Editor Laura McLaughlin gave it a 5 out of 5. She loved the firm seat cushion and how the chair managed to feel both stable and flexible.

“The back support specifically feels incredible, with firm yet comfortable padding and adjustable lumbar support,” she says.

At nearly 60 pounds, the chair is on the heavier side, and McLaughlin found it surprisingly difficult to roll around. That said, she felt that its weight contributed to how sturdy and supportive it was.

The Gesture can also support up to 400 pounds, just like the Steelcase Series 2, and is backed by a 12-year warranty, which is reassuring when you're spending four figures on an office chair.

If preserving your home’s interior design is top of mind, then the Branch Verve is minimalist with a unique flair and very comfortable. Made by the same brand as our top pick, this chair is $100 more and has fewer points of adjustment, but it also has a thick seat cushion and a breathable, beautifully designed 3D-knit back that comes in seven chic monochromatic looks.

You can adjust lumbar support, seat depth, and tilt for a decent fit. The chair comes with an optional headrest for $59 more, and the armrests are height-adjustable as well as removable. The chair itself is on the heavier side, weighing in at 40 pounds, but it’s also Greenguard Gold certified, which means it has been tested for volatile organic compounds and chemical emissions.

Read More: Best Standing Desks For Walking Pads

For those who struggle with back pain, a supportive office chair can be the difference between a productive workday and injury. The Steelcase Series 2 is the best option for those folks because it’s weight-activated—you just sit, and the chair’s back tension adjusts to you.

The thick seat cushion relieves pressure, and you can adjust the height, width, and depth of the armrests. (Most office chair armrests are just adjustable by height and sometimes width.) The chair can also support up to 400 pounds, which is about 100 pounds more than most of our picks. In terms of design, you can choose between a variety of colors, two frame colors, an optional headrest, and wheels for carpet or hard flooring.

Read More: Uplift Kneeling Ergonomic Chair Review

At under $500, the HON Ignition 2.0 is a budget office chair that still delivers in terms of support and adjustability. The chair itself is lightweight and easy to maneuver at under 25 pounds, and it sports a simple silhouette that won’t be an eyesore in your home office. The armrests can be raised and widened, and you can also easily adjust lumbar, tilt, and seat depth.

You can also opt to forgo armrests to bring the price closer to $400 or add a headrest and still keep the chair under the $600 threshold. The chair also comes backed by a limited lifetime warranty, which is unique for a high-quality home office chair. (For reference, the warranty on our top pick only lasts for seven years.)

At less than $100, the TikTok-famous Pukami Criss Cross Chair is a great option if you’re furnishing your home office on a budget. The extra-wide, foam-cushioned seat offers plenty of room to sit cross-legged, and its minimalist design and variety of color options make it easy to match with your home decor.

Despite its affordable price tag, the chair swivels, tilts, and can support up to 350 pounds. While it lacks the adjustable lumbar support, armrests, and wheels of our pricier picks, it’s worth considering if you work from home occasionally and don’t want to spend hundreds of dollars on an office chair.

Here are some key features to consider while you search for the best office chair for your body and needs.

Office chairs are not one-size-fits-all, which is why adjustability is crucial. “Adjustability lets the chair match your body so your spine stays in a neutral, supported position,” says Dr. Gbolohan Okubadejo, a spine surgeon and the head of The Institute of Comprehensive Spine Care. The lumbar support should match the curve of your spine, and your feet should be able to sit flat on the floor, according to Okubadejo.

“An unsupportive chair, or one that does not fit properly, can lead to chronic musculoskeletal injuries over time,” Lees says. “This may lead to pain that persists throughout the day, affecting sleep and stress levels. Long-term injuries may also include nerve damage that can lead to weakness or numbness.”

Most home office chairs are height adjustable and have armrests that can be raised. If a chair has a headrest, which isn’t essential, that may be adjustable as well. “Being able to tweak depth, tilt, and lumbar support prevents hot spots and improves blood flow during long sits.” Okubadejo says. “Small adjustments through the day break up static strain, so muscles don’t fatigue and posture doesn’t collapse.”

Lumbar refers to the lower back, and supporting this curve in your spine can relieve disc pressure and keep your pelvis in a neutral position, according to Okubadejo. “Good lumbar support lowers the risk of stiffness and pain during long hours at a desk,” he says.

Like chair height and seat cushioning, lumbar support will vary by person. “Postural muscles start to relax after a few minutes of sitting,” Lees says. “This leads to added stress on the spinal joints and extremity joints.” Luckily, many office chairs allow you to adjust the height and curve of the lumbar support. Okubadejo recommends options that can move up and down as well as in and out instead of stationary lumbar support.

The main components of a comfortable office chair are a sturdy frame, a thick seat cushion, and a supportive, breathable back. Most office chairs these days have a metal or plastic frame with a foam cushion and mesh back, although you can find upholstered and leather versions.

If you have the opportunity to test chairs in person, make sure that the seat is firm enough for you. “If the cushion is too soft, it won’t offer the support needed over time,” Lees says. “A cushion that is too firm could create pressure points and possibly affect blood flow in the legs.”

The materials of a chair can contribute to its overall weight and weight limit—both of which are important to keep in mind during your search.

Office chairs, like our top pick from Branch, can be beautiful in their own right but not necessarily as stylish as a sofa or armchair. Unfortunately, you may need to prioritize comfort over design when working from home, but you can opt for chairs with upholstery-like materials or lots of color options to marry the two.

Office chairs range in price from under $100 to more than $2,000, but you’ll find that most quality office chairs will cost around $500. It may seem like a lot to spend on a single chair, but it may also be your most-used piece of furniture outside of your bed and mattress if you work from home.

As a longtime remote worker and someone who suffers from chronic back pain, I’m particularly passionate about high-quality office chairs. When I set out to find the best home office chairs, I looked for a variety of models that would suit different body types, from height to weight. Supportive office chairs are easily adjustable, especially when it comes to seat height, armrest height, and lumbar support, so I wanted to highlight chairs that delivered on all three and beyond, with a few budget-friendly exceptions.

My top picks span a wide range of prices, from just $60 to a couple of luxury investment options over $1,500. Whether you’re starting a new remote job or desperately need to revamp your home office, these are the best home office chairs that will keep you comfortable and supported all day long.

#4838. CAT puts century-old train tech to work in its biggest underground machine yet

Diesel-electric locomotives have been barreling along America’s wide-open spaces for generations, and the century-old combination of highly efficient diesel engines spinning up generators to power high-torque electric motors has proven tough to beat. Now, Caterpillar is putting that century-old concept to work underground. Meet the CAT R3200 XE LHD.

One of the many hard-working machines moving chunks of Earth under your feet, an LHD (load, haul, and dump) machine is essentially a massive underground wheel loader designed to scoop up blasted rock, haul it through narrow mine tunnels, then dump it into trucks or ore passes. Built low and wide to fit in the tunnels, LHDs are workhorses of underground mining operations – and the new R3200 XE is CAT’s biggest yet, with a 25 ton payload and electric drive.

Before we get into the machine’s specs (the few that we have, anyway), I want to make sure understand that large-scale mining operations use obscene amounts of fuel, and a swing in site efficiency of just 1-2% can mean a huge difference in the bottom line – and fuel prices were up 27.4% (!) in August alone.

Keep the staggering weight of what that kind of fuel cost can mean to a fleet that buys fuel by the literal truckload as you read the rest of this.

Though not yet officially released by CAT, snippets of the company’s launch video have been leaking through dealers and trade journals, and they show the big machine powered by CAT’s newest 18.1 liter Tier 5 C18 diesel generator making 527 hp (~390 kW). That C18 reportedly sends electrons to the same electric drive system used in the company’s already successful 18-ton R2900 XE LHD.

In addition to a bigger generator and heftier payload, CAT says the upcoming R3200 XE LHD offers reduced cycle times versus the R2900 XE with 11% better speed on grade, plus reduced maintenance and repair costs thanks to design refinements for better durability, including redesigned axle. All told, that works out to 28% more tons per hour with 8% better fuel efficiency.

That efficiency is boosted by the same baked-in ADAS tech that’s made the smaller R2900 XE a favorite, and includes the latest version of CAT AutoDig and MineStar, ensuring that the machines are easy for experienced CAT operators to set up for remote, semi-autonomous, and even fully autonomous operation using Command for Underground.

We’ll post an update once CAT makes the full rundown of official specs public, which should be sooner rather than later. When that happens, we’ll see exactly how this big burrowing CAT stacks up against the competition from Sandvik, Epiroc, and Komatsu. In the meantime, let us know what you think of CAT’s newest electric drive machine in the comments.

#4837. The Evolution of Ab Training

The true path to six-pack abs (and IRL total-body stability) doesn’t involve just situps and planks. Why? Because your midsection can power much more.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

This is part of the Men's Health Body Bible, a collection of cutting-edge stories focused on helping you build more muscle using the latest science and lessons from some of the finest athletes and trainers on the planet.

THE SECRET TO training your abs is out—and it entails more than situps and planks, more than just targeting your rectus abdominis, the ballyhooed band of muscle between your chest and your hips. If you want true core strength (and, yes, that six-pack), a growing group of experts will tell you that you need to carry heavy weights and walk. This forces your core to constantly microcorrect and rebalance as you move, explains Aaron Horschig, C.S.C.S., D.P.T., a St. Louis–based physical therapist. You also need to twist and turn, challenging your oblique muscles and back extensors.

“While there’s nothing wrong with training the abs for show, training for stability—which encompasses all of the muscles that surround the spine and hips—is essential training for everyone,” says Horschig. His new book, Rebuilding Milo, includes a variety of exercises, many of which challenge your entire core—think lower back extensors, glutes, and obliques, which all team up with your abs to stabilize and bolster your back, lending postural support.

Unlike body parts that handle just one or two tasks (like your biceps, which are most heavily utilized to bend your elbows), all those core muscles have a host of responsibilities. They work together to flex your spine (as happens during a classic situp), and they help rotate your shoulders so you can turn to look at a friend. They also prevent excessive rounding of the lower back (known as anti-flexion), a key tactic in the battle to stop back pain. The ideal abs regimen trains all these functions, protecting you against injuries and readying your core (and spine) for anything life can throw at you. Horschig says people finally get that. “More and more people are starting to understand the true role of core,” he says.

The end result of all this work? A lower back that’s armor-plated against persistent pain, and the ability to move athletically and fluidly. And along the way, you’ll build those six-pack abs, too.

HOW TO DO IT:An underrated plank upgrade, this move challenges your abs and obliques (and your glutes, too!). Start in pushup position, feet wide. Lift your left hand and touch it to your right shoulder. Keep your hips square as you do. Repeat on the other side.

REPS & SETS:Work for time, not reps, doing three 40-second sets.

HOW TO DO IT:Stand in a split stance, left shoulder next to the high pulley of a cable machine, both hands grasping the handle, then bend at the knees until your left thigh is nearly parallel to the floor. Keep your hips square to the front as you pull the cable across your body, then return it to the start.

REPS & SETS:Do 10 to 12 reps per side. Do 3 sets.

HOW TO DO IT:Stand holding kettlebells in both hands, the left bell at your chest, the right bell at your hip. Walk forward (or march in place) for 10 to 15 steps per leg. Move slowly, working to keep your hips square.

REPS & SETS:Do 2 sets per side, challenging your abs and lower-back muscles to keep you upright against the heavy load.

TRAIN YOUR ABS EVERYDAY. Some muscle groups require several days to recover, but your core muscles are built to be resilient. That means you can train them nearly every day. Consider doing 3 or 4 sets of core work in every work- out, rotating in new and different ab exercises to continually challenge your rectus abdominis, oblique muscles, and lower-back spinal erectors.

NEVER GOING HEAVY. Bodyweight planks and situps are a solid starting point for your ab training. But just like any other muscle, core muscles are meant to be loaded and overloaded. Add resistance to your core training, and don’t be afraid to challenge yourself, especially on moves like the mixed-rack carry above. “You have to do that sometimes,” says the popular bodybuilder and trainer known as Ulisses Jr. “I’d be lying if I told you I didn’t load my abs.”

#4836. Obesity in Your 20s and 30s May Increase Cancer Risk Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Younger adults with obesity may be more likely to develop cancer before midlife than those who maintain a moderate weight, according to a study published on October 26 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

The risk for cancer became higher as weight increased. The highest rates were seen in those with severe obesity and abdominal obesity.

This highlights the potential importance of weight management in the prevention of early onset cancer.

Rates of both obesity and early onset cancer are rising among younger adults globally.

This study analyzed data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. The researchers identified 6,313,338 adults ages 20 to 39 who had no history of cancer and who underwent standardized national health screenings.

The researchers followed the participants for an average of 11 years.

Body mass index (BMI) was categorized into five groups ranging from underweight to class II obesity using the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for Asian populations. Waist circumference was also measured as an indicator of abdominal adiposity.

During the analysis, the researchers adjusted for various factors such as:

Over the follow-up period, there were 151,893 cases of cancer among the participants. The incidence rate increased progressively based on obesity categories, from 1.84% in “normal-weight” individuals to 2.24% in class I obesity and 2.62% in class II obesity.

The strongest associations were seen in the following cancers:

Obesity was not associated with breast cancer diagnosed before the age of 50.

Ketan Thanki, MD, board certified colorectal surgeon with the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, explained to Healthline that obesity itself causes states that promote cancer formation.

This current study focused on the Korean population. However, the connection between obesity and cancer risk is a global issue.

Previous research has shown that around 10% of all new cancer diagnoses in the United States are associated with obesity. Obesity also accounts for up to 50% of certain cancers, including endometrial and liver cancer.

The study also showed that waist circumference, which indicates abdominal obesity, may be linked to cancer risk that is similar to that of individuals with overweight.

The study researchers used the thresholds set out by the Korean Society for the Study of Obesity. These thresholds put the waist circumference cutoff at over 90 cm (35.4 in) for males and over 85cm (33.46 in) for females.

These are not universal cutoffs. According to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), waist circumference measurements that can increase your risk of negative health issues are 101.6 cm (40 in) for males and 88.9 cm (35 in) for females.

Previous research has also suggested an association between waist circumference and cancer risk, independent of BMI. One study showed a potential 11% increased risk of cancer in people with a waist circumference over the thresholds, even if they were physically active.

The current study found that males had a higher relative association between obesity and cancer, while females showed higher absolute risk.

The researchers also found that the absolute risk was higher in adults ages 30 to 39.

Those who currently smoke or who have ever smoked were also found to have a higher risk of developing cancer than those who have never smoked.

“Diet, exercise, and now medications can all be used very effectively to reduce one’s weight and, hopefully as a result, cancer risk,” Thanki said.

He also noted that, due to differences between South Korean populations and those in other countries such as the United States, further studies will be needed to determine how this translates across other populations.

“But I think this trend will likely extend across all cultures,” he said.

#4835. Polestar unveils Formula 2030 concept, previewing the next Polestar 2

Polestar has now fully unveiled the Formula 2030 concept, a low four-door electric sports car that previews the design of the next-generation Polestar 2 coming in 2027 and the Polestar 7 compact SUV.

The concept sits just 1,350 mm (53 inches) tall, which is lower than the Polestar 5 grand tourer, and it brings physical buttons back into the Swedish brand’s interior.

We reported in September that Polestar confirmed the Formula 2030 concept after showing it privately to investors and retailers in Gothenburg. Now we get the full set of pictures and the details.

It’s the first show car built under head of design Philipp Römers, who joined from Audi in 2024.

Polestar calls the Formula 2030 a “compact practical four-door sports car” that “sits within its own segment.” It’s 4,680 mm (184.3 inches) long and 2,021 mm (79.6 inches) wide, on a 2,780 mm (109.4-inch) wheelbase.

For context, that’s about 3 inches longer than today’s Polestar 2 and roughly 5 inches lower. It’s also a bit shorter than a Tesla Model 3 and sits 3.5 inches closer to the ground. Polestar says the concept lands “somewhere between” the upcoming Polestar 2 and Polestar 7 in size.

The proportions are classic sports car: long hood, short overhangs, the cabin pushed back over big rear haunches, and 22-inch center-lock wheels. There are gold Brembo calipers behind those wheels and Öhlins dampers on display in the trunk.

Up front, Polestar kept its “Dual Blade” headlights, now set into an aero wing over a shark nose and a deep splitter. The automaker says this is the face of the next-generation Polestar 2 planned for 2027.

There’s a single vertical windshield wiper, like on a race car, and a LiDAR unit that hides under an aerodynamic shroud and only shows itself when the car is driving autonomously.

The rear is where things change the most. Polestar dropped the full-width light bar, which is on just about every EV these days, for what it calls “Single Blade” rear lights. It says they are being introduced here “ahead of series production.”

Römers described the concept as a “bold evolution” of the brand’s existing design:

“It is a physical embodiment of how we apply Polestar’s core values of design, performance and sustainability to the next production cars.”

The rear doors are hinged at the back and there’s no B-pillar, so the whole side opens up to four individual seats.

The interior is built around the driver. A curved 20-inch display, which Polestar calls the “HyperDIM,” is mounted directly on the steering column, and a 12.2-inch center screen sits in the center tunnel.

But the bigger news is below that screen. Polestar added a panel of eight physical controls for the most-used functions, and owners could swap between types of controls, like rocker switches or rotary knobs, and program what each one does.

Polestar says it is “committing to rebalance the mix of physical and digital.” Juan Pablo Bernal, the company’s head of interior design, put it plainly:

“As a performance brand, we see a renewed focus on the driver, and so we re-balance the digital and physical. We introduce physical buttons and controls.”

That’s a big change for a brand whose recent cars run almost everything through the center touchscreen.

The cabin also physically changes with the drive mode. There are three of them: Performance, Normal, and Autonomous. In Performance, the center screen drops flush into the console and the steering wheel and its display pull closer to the driver. In Autonomous, the wheel and the seat move away from each other.

The four seats use inflatable bolsters that shape themselves to each occupant, and the seat backs are made of a flax-based composite instead of virgin plastic. Google Gemini is built in, like in Polestar’s production cars.

The cargo area is the strangest part of the car. The rear opens as a clamshell, and the trunk floor is transparent, with custom Polestar bags strapped down underneath it with gold straps.

Up front, the frunk holds two race helmets and a fire extinguisher, framed by a gold strut brace.

Now for what’s missing. Polestar didn’t release a single powertrain spec. No battery size, no range, no power output, and no price. This is a design study, and Polestar isn’t saying it will build it.

What it does say is that “various design attributes” from the concept will show up on the next Polestar 2 in 2027 and the Polestar 7 in 2028. Those are two of the four new models Polestar plans to launch in three years, and the 7 is going to be built in Europe.

Europe is where this matters, since Polestar is shut out of the US under the federal connected-vehicle rule. The concept made its debut during the media drive of the Polestar 4 SUV.

Polestar always impresses me with its design, and this is no exception with this new head of design.

The proportions are sharp. Long hood, cabin pushed back, big haunches, and a roofline lower than the Polestar 5’s on a car with four doors and four real seats. If the next Polestar 2 keeps even half of this stance, it’s going to be the best-looking car in its segment.

I have loved Polestar from the day they launched. Every car they design is a work of art and I love their commitment to transparency and sustainablitity. The 2023 Polestar 2 is still one of my favorite cars I've ever owned. I've driven the 3 and the 4 and both were fantastic. The fit and finish, ride and build quality, and NVH were all excellent. The upgraded 3 was probably going to be my next car in 2027 until they were forced to withdraw from the US. I think their future with the new 2 and 7 are bright and I'm still hoping (though I'm not holding my breath) that they will return to the US at some point. If the 5 was available here, I'd buy it today.

I don’t know about the trunk of this thing. Polestar itself calls the rear “UFO-esque,” and between the wraparound glass, the clamshell and the see-through floor, it’s a lot. But everything else on this car is pretty sharp.

Polestar is putting physical controls back in its cars and saying so in plain words. The way they talk about it makes it sound like you can expect that of upcoming production vehicles.

Now the usual caveat. A concept car doesn’t fix a balance sheet. Polestar lost $842 million in the first half of this year on a negative gross margin. Design has never been Polestar’s problem. Building these cars and selling them at a profit is.

#4834. Lucid says service wait times fell 20% after 40% jump in service staff

Lucid (LCID) says service wait times dropped 20% globally in the third quarter after it grew its technician and service-support staff by more than 40% in a single quarter.

The automaker is also adding Studio and Service Centers in Southern California, Los Angeles, Dallas, and the Chicago suburbs, plus 20 more Gravity Mobile Service vans. It’s a clear sign that service had become a problem for Lucid owners.

Lucid announced the numbers today, a day after its Q3 2026 earnings. Both comparisons are against the second quarter, not a year ago.

The hiring isn’t done either. After a 40%-plus increase in technicians, advisors, and concierges in Q3, Lucid wants that figure at 50% by the end of 2026 and 60% by Q1 2027. Mobile Service capacity in North America grew 15%, with a 40% target for year-end.

That’s a big hiring push for a company that laid off 18% of its workforce in June, its second cut in four months after a 12% reduction in February. Roughly 1,500 people left across those two rounds.

And owners noticed. On the LucidOwners forum, one Air Touring owner posted in early October that Lucid told them in writing to expect “a service time of about 7 weeks” at its Beverly Hills Service Center. Other threads blamed service-department layoffs for slow repairs and recall work.

Billy Hayes, Lucid’s Chief Customer Officer, said the company is “adding service personnel, and increasing Mobile Service capacity to reduce wait times and provide more convenient, responsive support.”

Here’s what’s opening, according to Lucid:

Lucid is also letting a growing number of its Certified Collision shops handle recall campaign work, which should take some pressure off its own Service Centers.

Outside the US, the expansion leans on partners. Munsterhuis Autobedrijven is Lucid’s first retail partner in the Netherlands (Hengelo), Cloppenburg Automobil SE opens a Duisburg retail and service site in January 2027, Autohaus Possögel starts authorized service in Naumburg, Germany, in December, and Emil Frey France will support Lucid’s launch in France. In Saudi Arabia, Lucid opened its first company-owned Body & Paint Repair Center in Riyadh, with more service sites in Riyadh and Dammam coming in the first half of 2027.

Lucid doesn’t say what the average wait time actually is.

A 20% drop from seven weeks is still more than five weeks. A 20% drop from one week is a non-issue. Without a baseline, owners can’t tell which one they’re getting.

It’s also hard to separate better service from fewer cars coming in. Lucid delivered 3,806 vehicles in Q3, down 7% year-over-year, while it worked through inventory. Its fleet keeps growing, but slowly.

For context, Rivian delivered 19,248 vehicles in Q3, five times Lucid’s volume, and it’s been leaning hard on mobile service too. Lucid is a much smaller operation trying to cover the US, Europe, and the Middle East with a thin network.

This is the right move, and it’s overdue.

Lucid has been one of the few EV startups with genuinely class-leading hardware. The Air’s efficiency is still unmatched and the Gravity is a great vehicle on paper, even if we found its software wasn’t ready. But when you’re asking someone to spend $80,000 or more on a car from a brand with an uncertain future, the ownership experience is half the sale. A seven-week wait for a repair kills that sale, and the referrals that come after it.

So growing service staff by 40% in a quarter is a big deal. It also tells you how thin those teams had gotten after two rounds of layoffs. Lucid cut too deep in the wrong place, and it’s now hiring to fix it.

The problem is the timing and the money. Lucid burned $1.04 billion in free cash flow in Q3 and only stays funded into late 2027 because the PIF just added another $1.75 billion. Meanwhile, the Midsize “Cosmos” that’s supposed to bring real volume doesn’t start production until the second half of 2027. Service is exactly where Lucid should spend between now and then, because the buyers it has today are the ones who’ll decide whether anybody trusts the brand with a cheaper EV.

#4833. Unit1 FARO and NEON review: I just found my new favorite e-bike helmets

I test a lot of electric bikes, which means I also spend a lot of time wearing bicycle helmets. And while most helmets tend to fall into the decidedly unexciting category of “necessary safety equipment,” UNIT 1 has managed to make a couple that I actually get excited about wearing.

I’ve been using both the UNIT 1 FARO and the new NEON, and despite taking fairly different approaches, they’ve both become regular go-to helmets for me.

The FARO is the more futuristic-looking of the two, and it’s also the one that really leans into the “smart helmet” concept.

The helmet includes MIPS protection to reduce rotational impact during a collision, as well as integrated lighting on both the front and rear, including a large customizable rear lighting area made up of dozens of LEDs.

That large rear LED array is a feature I particularly appreciate since visibility is such a major part of cycling safety.

A helmet obviously can’t force drivers to pay attention, but I’d rather give them as many opportunities as possible to see me. The hidden light area below the obvious LED light bar adds a lot of extra visibility.

You can see just how vivid it is in the GIF below, though in real life it looks even better!

The FARO’s lighting system works with UNIT 1’s handlebar remote, which adds turn signals controlled right from the bars.

The system can also provide automatic brake-light functionality, giving you another way to communicate with traffic around you.

I’ll admit that turn signals on bicycles can sometimes feel a bit gimmicky, especially when they’re so close together that drivers can’t really tell which direction is flashing. But putting them high up on the helmet makes them considerably more visible, and the little wireless handlebar remote makes operating them incredibly easy.

The rechargeable lighting is also convenient. I’ve topped up the helmet from a power bank while out and about, meaning you don’t necessarily need to find a wall outlet if you realize your helmet is running low. The rear LED light bar also turns green and illuminates along the length of the bar to let you know what percentage of charge the battery has reached. The only way it could be clearer would be with a screen, but we’re still talking about a helmet here, not a phone.

There are other smart features packed in too, including crash detection and app-based customization.

The tradeoff is weight. At around 640 grams for a medium, the FARO is noticeably heavier than a conventional bicycle helmet. It doesn’t bother me much once I’m riding, and I’ve found the helmet comfortable, but you definitely know there’s more helmet up there. Each time I pick it up, I’m reminded that it’s not just the basic little foam shell that I’ve been wearing for the last few years.

Then there’s the price. At around $230 (or $195 during the current Black Friday sale period), this isn’t a cheap helmet. You’re paying for all of that technology, lighting, and design.

As much as I like the FARO, I’ve also become a big fan of the UNIT 1 NEON.

At roughly 430 grams in a medium, it’s significantly lighter than the FARO, and that difference is immediately noticeable. It’s also a bit cheaper at around $210 (or $178 during the Black Friday sale period) while still packing several of the smart features that make UNIT 1’s helmets interesting.

You still get MIPS rotational protection, crash detection, integrated rear lighting, app connectivity, and compatibility with UNIT 1’s handlebar remote for turn signals and brake-light functionality.

I do wish the NEON had a front light like the FARO. That’s probably the biggest feature I miss when switching between the two. But the NEON makes up for it with one of my favorite features on either helmet: its magnetic face shield.

The shield is ridiculously easy to attach and remove. You don’t even need to carefully line it up. I just need to get it somewhere near the mounting points with one hand and the powerful magnets basically grab it out of the air and snap it into position.

That means I can easily add or remove it one-handed, even while riding.

The photochromic shield is clear enough for night riding but darkens when exposed to bright sunlight, giving you sun protection without requiring separate daytime and nighttime shields. I’ve found that incredibly convenient, especially on rides that transition from daylight into evening. I hate that I can’t wear my sunglasses for eye protection at night, and a lens like this solves that issue.

The NEON also gets something particularly important for faster e-bike riders: NTA 8776 certification. That’s the Dutch standard designed specifically around higher-speed e-bike uses at up to 45 km/h (28 mph). For the Class 3 e-bikes that have become increasingly common in the US, that’s a big distinction compared to helmets rated for crashes at slower speeds.

That’s actually difficult, because I regularly use both.

The FARO is the one I’d choose if maximum visibility and technology were my priorities. I love having LEDs both front and rear, the MIPS protection, and the handlebar-controlled turn signals. It’s comfortable, looks great, and has become one of my favorite urban riding helmets.

But the NEON may be the easier helmet to recommend to most e-bike riders.

It’s lighter, a little cheaper, still gives you a rear light and smart safety features, has that excellent magnetic photochromic face shield, and importantly carries NTA 8776 certification for faster e-bike riding.

Neither helmet is inexpensive, and the FARO in particular asks you to accept some extra weight in exchange for all that technology. But I’m used to wearing much heavier motorcycle helmets and ways.

Plus, it’s important to note that these aren’t helmets I tested for a few rides and then tossed onto a shelf. Both have stayed in my regular rotation, and I find myself reaching for them frequently when I head out on an e-bike. The fact that I not only enjoyed them during my testing but actually replaced my old helmets with them should speak for itself.

For someone who rides as much as I do, that’s probably the strongest endorsement I can give them.

Between solid helmets like these and safe riding clothing, it’s good to feel protected!

#4832. Letter From the Editor-in-Chief: What a Decade of Bedtime Stories Taught Me About Health

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

I’ve read to my children each night at bedtime for as long as I (and they) can remember. We started with the likes of “Goodnight Batcave” and the lesser-known-in-the-US but oh-so-wonderful collection of verse-driven classics from former UK Children’s Laureate Julia Donaldson.

We moved on to B.J. Novak’s anarchic love letter to the power of words (and to great typography), “The Book With No Pictures.”

We eventually worked our way up to Roald Dahl’s wickedly dark back catalog, discovering more complex characters, language and plotting as we went.

When my eldest, Amelia, hit 6, it was time to roll out the big guns.

Over the last 5 years (she’s now 11), I’ve read the seven Harry Potter books aloud twice, complete with all the voices: once to Amelia on her own, once to both her and her brother, Henry, two years her junior.

I had feared she wouldn’t be keen on another helping, but Amelia immersed herself once more in the world of Hogwarts with no hesitation and took immense joy in watching Henry discover for himself every twist and turn on Harry’s journey.

We have done the same thing with Tolkien’s “The Hobbit” and his fantasy masterpiece “The Lord of the Rings,” and are currently midway through “The Two Towers” on our second go around.

There’s a huge amount of reciprocal joy we take from this nightly ritual, beyond the practical benefits of providing a calming demarcation between the end of the day and the wind-down to sleep.

For me, it comes as either a break in my working day or a signal that it’s over, depending on how hectic things are.

For the kids, it’s an all-too-rare chance to get me all to themselves, no deadlines, screens, or other distractions to pull me away from being anything but 100% present.

For all three of us, it’s a literal (and literary!) warm blanket — a chance to escape under the covers to familiar worlds and familiar faces. It is, in short, incredibly good for our well-being.

And yet, in the world of health information — including on this site — thousands, if not millions, of reading hours are dedicated to the benefits of nutrition, sleep, and exercise as the building blocks of good health. Reading itself rarely makes that shortlist.

For me, it unequivocally deserves a place on it. Research seems to support that case. Even if we need more of it to really understand how and why.

A recent editorial in Psychological Medicine co-authored by Barbara Sahakian, Professor of Clinical Neuropsychology at Cambridge University, draws on a broad range of research linking reading for pleasure to better mental health and greater empathy.

The positive impact of reading on young people — just like Amelia and Henry — also carries evidence.

Among more than 10,000 US adolescents, those who started reading for pleasure early had fewer mental health problems, spent less time on screens and slept more. Although, per an earlier column of mine, I can’t vouch for the sleep side of things when it comes to early bird Henry.

For many, reading can be a form of therapy that improves well-being. Bibliotherapy is a complementary therapeutic tool for emotional release and reduced stress and anxiety, with its roots traced back to ancient civilizations.

There’s even research suggesting a link between a love of reading and a lower risk of cognitive decline.

In a 2003 study of people aged 75 and over, reading was associated with a 35% lower risk of dementia over roughly five years.

A separate 14-year study from 2022 found that people who read at least weekly saw less cognitive decline, whatever their level of education.

A happy (and healthy) by-product of this love of being read to is that both my kids have now started reading to me at bedtime. Henry recently read “Jeffy the Burglar’s Cat” to us, a lesser-known but no less compelling chapter book by Ursula Moray Williams that was a staple of my own childhood. And we’ve enjoyed several books from Amelia, including the wistful tale of friendship and the circle of life, “Charlotte’s Web” by E.B. White – not a dry eye in the house for the final few chapters of that one.

They’ve also gone off and re-read the Harry Potter books and “The Hobbit” to themselves.

The research above links reading to many health benefits: better attention and memory, fewer mental health problems, more sleep, less time on screens, and greater empathy. I haven’t measured any of those impacts empirically in our house. Nor am I naive to the fact that as they get older, they’ll ultimately grow out of me reading to them, with school, extracurricular activities, their friends, and inevitably screens competing for more and more of their time.

Come what may, though, I know that a child who considers missing a reading session as the most cardinal of cardinal sins, and who scrambles for the chance to read aloud to their dad at bedtime is, at that moment, concentrating, empathizing, discovering and growing.

Researchers are clear that studies espousing the benefits of reading show association rather than proof, and it’s evident that more experimental work and deeper research are needed to ensure the complex cause and effect stands on firm scientific ground.

Regardless, it’s a healthy habit Amelia, Henry and I are very happy to keep, and with a bit of luck, I’ll get to pass it on to their kids one day.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4831. With Age Comes a Unique Ability to Harness the Power of AI

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Co-authored by George S. Everly, Jr., PhD, MA, ABPP, and Barry McGovern, Solutions Engineer, JBS International

Today, November 19, 2026, is an important day in the world of artificial intelligence (AI). Anthropic, a major artificial intelligence company, is beginning to sell ownership shares of stock in the company to the public. At the same time, Anthropic’s founder, Dario Amodei, issued a warning. He cautioned that AI is developing more rapidly than expected, especially through the process of recursive self-improvement, which allows the programs to improve themselves without human guidance.

We often look to younger generations when it comes to guidance regarding AI. Perhaps surprisingly, older generations may have much to offer in managing and directing AI, especially at the level of personal use. Decades of lived experience, pattern recognition, and knowing how to ask the right questions allow older generations to harness the power of AI through the process of “prompt engineering” in a way that is more mature and experience-informed than it is for younger generations.

On average, older adults (age 50 or older) are more skeptical of artificial intelligence (AI), less trusting of its responses to questions, and less likely to use it than younger adults. While caution is warranted, older adults possess a hidden “superpower” in the form of prompt engineering based upon lived experience that, at least at this point, allows them to become active managers of AI rather than non-critical users, overly cautious passive recipients, or worse yet, non-participants. Ironically, this “superpower” is more prevalent in older adults than younger adults and may increase to some degree with age.

For adults aged 18-40, the use of AI is likely 70 percent or higher. However, survey research conducted by AARP (AARP, September 23, 2025) found that familiarity with and use of AI decrease with age. About 47 percent of adults in their 50s reported knowing about and using AI, compared with 25 percent of those over 70.

As described in a previous post, AI may encourage passive, non-critical consumption of information. The risks of such passive consumption have yet to be fully determined, but AI may lead to the inhibition of critical thinking and the creation of a functional dependence. A recent TV commercial showed a character gleefully stating that she has difficulty thinking without AI. It is this very passivity that increases the risk of an untethered AI.

Younger users may seem to treat AI like an answer machine because they don't yet have the foundational knowledge to critically assess the validity of the information provided. Older adults, by contrast, have a built-in "lie-detector” from decades of career and life experience—in short, they know what a valid answer is supposed to look like and may be better positioned than younger adults to ask follow-up questions that can challenge AI.

Francis Bacon once noted, “If a man will begin with certainties, he shall end in doubts; but if he will be content to begin with doubts, he shall end in certainties.” So far, the errors or “overzealousness” exhibited by AI appear to be related to the questions asked of it. The more vague or less structured the questions, and the more repetitive the questions posed to AI, the greater its tendency to try to anticipate the desired answer and to “please” the questioner by “hallucinating” and creating spurious evidence to support the desired conclusions even though incorrect. In addition, AI does not possess the ability to independently assess the validity of the data it retrieves nor its recombinant output. As such, it may provide misleading or erroneous information.

The aging process is often accompanied by the accumulation of insights, knowledge, and informative experiences. These attributes may reveal themselves as the “superpower” ability to formulate specific, targeted questions. Rather than fostering passive consumption, knowledge and experience can foster informed, active consumption. It fosters the potential for a complementary, if not synergistic, relationship with AI wherein the person formulates knowledge- and experience-informed questions that not only target the efforts of AI but can serve as a series of checks and balances through AI’s recombinant efforts to provide answers.

For instance, a younger, less experienced person might ask AI, "Write me a business plan" (passive, vague), while a 60-year-old might ask, "Construct a business plan that overcomes these three most common reasons new tech companies fail" (experience-driven, targeted). Or, the less experienced consultant might ask AI, “Write an independent contractor’s agreement” (vague, too general), as opposed to “Create an independent contractor’s agreement that ensures the ownership of my pre-existing intellectual property does not transfer as a work for hire” (very specific, anticipating potential confusion over ownership).

Socrates believed the highest form of wisdom arose from introspection and self-reflection. Just as he used questions to challenge his students to provide the best answers to the most pressing questions of his day, perhaps we can harness questions in the Socratic method to guide AI to provide us with the answers to the most pressing questions of our day.

#4830. Tesla’s China sales crash 66% to lowest level in over four years

Only 8,817 of the cars Tesla delivered from Giga Shanghai in October went to Chinese buyers. That’s down 66% from a year ago and Tesla’s worst month in China since July 2022, according to CPCA data.

Back in July 2022, the Shanghai factory was partly shut down for line upgrades. This time it ran normally and shipped 87% of what it built out of the country.

The China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) reported that Tesla China wholesaled 67,829 vehicles in October, up 10.3% year-over-year. That’s the number most headlines ran with.

But 59,012 of those were exports. Strip them out and you’re left with 8,817 cars for the domestic market, the one Giga Shanghai was originally built to serve.

Nearly all of them were Model Ys (7,807), according to CnEVPost, leaving just 1,010 Model 3s. And compared to September, when Tesla sold 64,837 cars in China, domestic sales fell 86%.

Here’s how October has looked over the last three years:

Tesla favors export orders early in each quarter and pushes domestic deliveries toward the end of it, and September’s promotions and quarter-end rush pulled some demand forward.

That’s real. Tesla’s China sales have followed this sawtooth pattern for years. Last October was also weak, and Tesla then delivered 73,145 cars in China in November and 93,843 in December.

But it doesn’t explain the size of this drop. Here’s every first month of a quarter in 2026:

October is less than half of the previous low this year. And the October trough keeps getting deeper: 40,485 in 2024, 26,006 in 2025, 8,817 now.

China’s EV market is having a rough year. NEV retail sales fell 10% year-over-year in October to 1.148 million units, according to CPCA’s preliminary data, as Beijing phases out trade-in subsidies and the NEV purchase tax exemption was cut in half on January 1. The overall passenger car market was down 25%.

Tesla was down 66%. That works out to about 0.8% of China’s NEV retail market last month.

Meanwhile, Xiaomi, which only started delivering cars in 2024, delivered more than 50,000 vehicles in October. Leapmotor delivered 106,127, up 51%. BYD delivered 490,168, though that includes its exports.

Through October, Tesla has sold 389,905 cars in China. That’s down 15% from 458,710 over the same period last year and its lowest January-to-October total in at least four years:

The decline is speeding up. Tesla was down 11.9% in China through September, and one bad October pushed that to 15%. This year is now 22% below the 2024 peak, or about 110,000 fewer cars.

Exports from Giga Shanghai went the other way, up 101% to 420,984.

So this year, Shanghai has now shipped more cars abroad than it sold at home. Last year, domestic sales beat exports by more than two to one.

As we reported last month, Beijing is cutting the VAT export rebate on EVs from 13% to 9% on April 1, 2027, with the rate set by the customs declaration date. We said to expect automakers to cram exports in ahead of the deadline. October’s 59,012 exports, up 66% year-over-year, fit that.

We’ve been tracking this gap all year, from Tesla’s Q1 China retail crash to the first-half numbers. Every time, the wholesale headline looks fine and the domestic number underneath gets worse. October is the most extreme version yet: Tesla China “grew” 10% while Chinese buyers bought 66% fewer Teslas.

We don’t buy that this is just the quarterly cycle. The cycle explains why October is weaker than September. It doesn’t explain why this October is a third of last October, or less than half of any other month this year.

I've been saying this for the last two years. Tesla's problem isn't that Elon temporarily alienated customers in Europe or other countries. Yes that killed sales for a bit, but in the end people are practical and will buy the best car for the money. And we saw that is exactly what happened with European Tesla sales coming back when gas prices rose and Tesla as a package (quality + price) was still very competitive.

The real problem that Tesla has is that they're falling behind in China not because anyone cares about Elon's politics, but because the cars are just less and less competitive. And while the Chinese competition doubles down on vehicle development and rolls out a new car every week, Tesla has lost all interest in it. There is absolutely nothing on the horizon for them in terms of new vehicles that consumers can buy. Looks like the 3 and Y are all they will have and no updates are coming.

I know, FSD or bust, but that's also assuming Chinese brands don't crack that nut at the same time.

Two things can be true at once. The export numbers show Tesla front-loading shipments ahead of the rebate cut. And Chinese demand for a Model 3 and Model Y lineup that hasn’t fundamentally changed in years keeps fading while Xiaomi, Leapmotor and BYD launch new models every few months.

And if Tesla is choosing to send cars abroad instead of selling them in China, that’s not exactly a vote of confidence in its Chinese business either.

The real test is November and December. Last year, Tesla bounced back to 73,000 and 94,000 domestic sales. If it gets close to that again, October was mostly timing. If it doesn’t, Tesla has a serious problem in the world’s largest EV market, and the export valve that’s been hiding it gets more expensive in April.

#4829. This bear’s big butt is so beautiful, it just won an award

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 10, 2026 3:13 PM EST

Yes, bears are big. Depending on the time of year and sex, the average black bear (Ursus americanus) weighs between 90 to 500 pounds. On average brown bears (Ursus arctos) can weigh between 600 to 900 pounds. However, one female black bear named Volverine is a true fat bear queen this year. The U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska have awarded her with the 2026 Big & Beautiful Award for her heft.

The rangers say that this mother bear is a “true icon,” who will often pose on a rock for a long time, seemingly allowing the visitors to Anan Wildlife Observatory to take photos. She is regarded as one of the most beautiful bears at Anan, with a chest patch shaped like the letter V. Volverine is also on the bigger end of the black bear spectrum, with a potato-shaped body, and an especially round butt. Her fishing skills made her one of the largest bears of the 2026 season—and a dominant matriarch.

“Our rangers love to see a fat female bear because that could mean cubs next year!” the rangers write. “Bears have what’s called delayed implantation, meaning they mate in the spring, and IF they get fat enough, the embryos implant in the fall.”

Wishing Volverine and all of the bears the best this winter season.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. The run is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears. Like their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks. Volverine would fit right in with Katmai’s chunky brown bears, despite the fact that black bears tend to be a bit smaller.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of what they are up to 24/7.

#4828. The coolest ride in town is England’s first electric ice cream truck

The “world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer” has released its first fully electric ice cream truck, which is already in operaiton, and it says it’s open for orders for more.

Whitby Morrison bills itself as “the world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer,” supplying converted vans as ice cream trucks to drivers worldwide.

And now it has taken a big step into the modern age delivering its first fully electric ice cream truck to Hocking’s dairy in North Devon, England.

The truck has been operating since July, through the course of one “ice cream season.” It reportedly covered more than 100 miles a day and has done days serving up to 12 hours at a time.

It’s built on a standard Mercedes eSprinter, so it’s not retrofitted from the diesel vans that make up most of Whitby Morrison’s other offerings. The eSprinter comes in a “chassis cab” configuration which comes with just the chassis and cab, and lets upfitters build whatever they want onto the back end of the vehicle.

In this case, it also got some pretty extensive (and a little over-the-top) art all around the vehicle, highlighting the van’s electric operation.

The ice cream truck maker, Whitby Morrison, says this is the “world’s first fully certified electric ice cream truck.”

We’re not sure what sort of international certifications are required for an ice cream truck so we’ll take their word for it, but we have seen a Rivian EDV turned into a Ben & Jerry’s ice cream truck, complete with side window, and a concept electric ice cream truck as far back as 2019. So it’s certainly not the very first time this idea has been had, at least.

And it is a good idea. As with school buses, ice cream trucks are vehicles that children are likely to congregate around. Having a stinky old truck spewing emissions just a few feet away from those kids’ lungs is the sort of thing that can expose them to a life of health problems… and we might as well not stack that on top of the sugar addiction we’re teaching them to have (hey, at least they have to get outside to chase the truck down, so they’re getting some physical activity out of it, right?)

It also opens up more possibilities for operators to serve at events where having a diesel truck running might not be reasonable, like in enclosed spaces or where quiet might be appreciated (this came up when we went to Harbinger Motors’ factory opening, where local food trucks were in attendance, inside the large factory building, and made the air quality noticeably worse).

Whitby Morrison says it’s taking orders both in the UK and overseas, with US orders just opening. To learn more, head on over to its website.

#4827. How to Prevent Arguments at Thanksgiving Dinner

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

The days leading up to Thanksgiving can feel like a whirlwind. Between figuring out who’s bringing what and dodging holiday traffic, nerves can wear thin before the first guest arrives. The extra leaf has to be wrestled out of the closet to stretch the table a little longer, and someone has been up since dawn coaxing the turkey toward golden. By the time everyone sits down, the coats are piled high on a bed down the hall and someone is sneaking a roll before grace. Then, somewhere between the first helping and the pie, a loaded remark cuts across the table and the tension becomes palpable. We spend weeks preparing the meal, yet the conversations shared over it rarely receive the same forethought.

Over the years, journalists have asked me how to keep Thanksgiving conversations from boiling over, and I always say we can’t control what others say or do, but we can choose how we respond. The key is remembering the person across the table matters more than proving a point.

Before the gathering, it helps to take inventory of ourselves. I think of it like packing for a trip somewhere new. We check the forecast and pack for the weather we expect, knowing the skies can still shift once we land. In the same way, we can reflect on which topics might feel sensitive this year.

If some relatives tend to bring up challenging subjects, a quick heads-up can make those conversations easier to navigate. We might say, “I’ve been looking forward to being together, and it would mean a lot if we could keep things lighter this year.” Sharing this means everyone can arrive on the same page and enjoy one another’s company.

Thanksgiving conversations have a way of wandering into topics no one meant to open. A comment lands the wrong way and suddenly we’re deciding whether to let it go or respond. A racing heart can be a cue to take a breath and pause. In that pause, we can ask ourselves three questions:

These questions can help us decide how, if at all, to engage. If the answer to any of them is no, we can steer the conversation toward common ground. We don’t have to follow every conversation into the weeds. Sometimes the kindest thing we can do for a conversation is to decide not to have it.

At the same time, steering clear of hard topics isn’t always the answer. A difficult conversation doesn’t have to strain our relationships. Research on Thanksgiving discussions suggests that college students whose families encouraged open conversation reported more positive effects on family closeness and less stress afterward.

A disagreement does not have to become an argument. Much depends on whether we are trying to prove a point or to understand someone. Scholarship on serial arguments indicates that people often care more about working things out together than gaining the upper hand. Arguments tend to take hold once difference feels like a threat, pulling us into an either/or mindset where one view must prevail over the other. To stay on the side of understanding, we can ask ourselves, “How can I express my views while still showing respect and valuing this person?” If a conversation feels uncomfortable, we might say, “I hear you, and I hold a different perspective.” Sentiments like these help others feel heard, even when we see things differently.

Of course, it wouldn’t be Thanksgiving without someone bringing up that topic—the one half the family has been hoping to avoid. We try to change the subject, and for a few minutes the conversation moves on to football and Black Friday deals. Then, just as everyone relaxes, that same relative finds a way back to the topic. It’s understandable to feel frustrated, yet shutting down the conversation can create more distance. After all, this is someone who matters to us, and there may be something more going on beneath the surface.

Difficult conversations can be complex webs of unspoken needs and hidden emotions. Maybe our relative is trying to make sense of something they’re going through, or looking for connection without knowing how to express that need. They may feel anxious or unheard. Or, there may be reasons we haven’t considered at all.

Without fully knowing the reason, some thoughtfulness can go a long way. It’s worth considering the experiences that may be influencing their viewpoint. Stepping into another’s shoes, even for a moment, can foster understanding and empathy. Offered sincerely, an affirmation such as “I can tell how much you care about this” conveys they are seen and heard, which can change the tone of the whole conversation.

Other times, we watch from the sidelines as two relatives barrel toward an argument we all saw coming. Family arguments often gain momentum through the quick volley of replies, each one arriving a little faster and a little louder than the last. Before long, the momentum takes over in ways the original comment never would have on its own.

In situations like these, we can interrupt the pace, not the people. A calm invitation such as “This feels a little tense. Maybe we can pause this for now” can slow things down, and families tend to respond more openly to understanding than to judgment. Asking a relative to help carry dishes to the kitchen or check on the pie breaks the rhythm without putting anyone on the spot, giving each person a graceful way to step back with their dignity intact. The goal isn’t to referee or get everyone to agree, but to give the whole table a chance to reset.

Keeping the peace at Thanksgiving doesn’t require everyone to share the same point of view, and understanding someone else’s doesn’t mean giving up our own. We can, however, choose how we treat one another, even when we disagree.

Bevan, J. L. (2010). Serial argument goals and conflict strategies: A comparison between romantic partners and family members. Communication Reports, 23(1), 52–64. doi.org/10.1080/08934211003598734

Johnson, A. J., Bostwick, E. N., & Cionea, I. A. (2019). Talking turkey: Effects of family discussions about the 2016 election over the Thanksgiving holiday. Journal of Family Communication, 19(1), 63–76. doi.org/10.1080/15267431.2018.1543688

#4826. College student develops LEGO-like, 3D-printed moon bricks

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 10, 2026 4:30 PM EST

A permanent lunar base will require structures resilient enough to withstand everything from cosmic radiation and micro-meteorites to moonquakes. There are plenty of building materials to choose from on Earth, but they all come with a catch: transportation storage aboard spacecraft is limited, and each additional pound of cargo will quickly ramp up costs. Engineers have spent years experimenting with ways for future astronauts to source local lunar ingredients, including fine moon dust known as regolith. Unfortunately, most require various binding ingredients that must still be sent from back home.

A college student at the University of Arkansas (U of A) recently had a different idea. In a collaboration with U of A mechanical engineer Wan Shou, Cole McCallum harnessed a specialized method of 3D printing to manufacture LEGO-esque bricks from lunar dust, no binding required. (These aren’t to be confused with LEGO’s actual lunar bricks mockups). Their results published in the journal NPJ Advanced Manufacturing indicate the bricks could be a promising material to investigate as humanity readies itself for a return to the moon.

Lunar regolith is a tricky material. Unlike Earth’s dirt, it doesn’t contain any amount of organic matter. It’s just loose, sharp-edged particles generated by billions’ of years of asteroid and meteor impacts. This means that moon dust can’t bind on its own and requires at least some secondary ingredients.

While an undergraduate at the U of A, McCallum wondered if a specific type of 3D printing called laser powder bed fusion could offer a workaround. In this technique, fine powder is placed on a flat bed, then exposed to a highly powerful laser beam that fuses each microscopic particle together in a process called sintering. The tray bed lowers down to allow another layer of sintered powder, then repeats the steps until a single, solid block is created. Regolith fits the mold perfectly, so to speak.

“There’s nothing else it’s binding to. The regolith powder is binding to itself,” McCallum said in a university profile.

McCallum and Shou didn’t have access to actual lunar material, so they obtained Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant (LHS-1), a commercial material that replicates the moon dust collected by Apollo astronauts during the 1960s and 70s. They ultimately settled on two shapes, one that resembles a cross and another that looks like the letter “H.” The researchers then 3D-printed tiny prototypes measuring a few centimeters wide that they could connect like LEGOs to construct larger structures.

There are still some important caveats to this sintered regolith strategy. McCallum’s blocks are much more porous and weaker than materials containing binders. Additional research is needed to see how the approach works in a vacuum or microgravity, two inescapable hurdles to living on the moon.

“These structures we’re making can be self-supported. But I would be hesitant to say our process could be used for something that’s supporting other loads at this moment yet,” said McCallum.

That said, his demonstration that even a basic framework for lunar base bricks is achievable solely with regolith may offer a promising direction for mission engineers

#4825. How Non-Dairy Creamers Doubled Coffee’s Calories For Many Americans

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Coffee consumption among U.S. adults remained relatively stable between 2003 and 2018, but the average number of calories consumed from coffee beverages increased by nearly 40%, according to a study published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.

By 2017–2018, U.S. adults consumed an average of about 13 ounces of coffee beverages per day. Meanwhile, the average daily calorie intake from these beverages had increased from 43 to 60 calories since 2003–2004.

By 2018, non-dairy creamer had become the largest source of calories added to coffee, surpassing sugar or syrup and dairy milk.

The researchers analyzed data from eight consecutive cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2003 to 2018. The study included 30,459 U.S. adults ages 20 and older who provided two 24-hour dietary recalls.

The researchers categorized coffee beverages based on whether they contained added ingredients. These additions included:

The researchers found that coffee intake remained stable, while the average calorie intake from coffee beverages increased.

The absolute increase in caloric intake is about 17 kcal per day, which is only about 1% of a 2,000 kcal diet.

Coffee consumption was also higher among men, non-Hispanic white adults, and people with higher incomes. Those who slept fewer hours or worked longer hours also tended to drink more coffee.

In 2018, the most common coffee additions by weight were:

The researchers found no significant changes in the amounts of dairy milk, sugar or syrup, and sugar substitutes added to coffee between 2003 and 2018.

However, consumption of non-dairy additions increased during this period. Non-dairy creamer consumption rose from 3.37 to 8.08 grams per day, while non-dairy milk increased from 0.27 to 2.45 grams per day.

By 2017–2018, non-dairy creamer contributed the most calories among coffee additions:

In 2003–2004, non-dairy creamer contributed an average of 7.7 calories per day, meaning its calorie contribution more than doubled by 2017–2018.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, president of KAK, Consulting, LLC, and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Cleveland, Ohio, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings didn’t surprise her.

“The variety of coffee drinks, both at coffee houses and grocery stores, as well as options for creamers in the grocery store, make it easy to trade in black coffee for something closer to dessert,” she said.

She also added, however, that not all non-dairy creamers are created equal.

“Some are quite natural, with minimal ingredients, including no added sugars and no additives. Others are ingredient-heavy with either a large amount of sugar (real or artificial) and additives, so it’s really based on the type that is purchased,” she noted.

More than 60% of Americans drink coffee daily. Research suggests that drinking coffee with little to no added sugar or saturated fat may offer health benefits.

Previous research has associated moderate coffee consumption, typically around 3–5 cups per day, with a lower risk of several health conditions, including:

“These benefits make sense. After all, coffee beans are indeed a deeply hued plant, with multiple bioactive compounds that may strengthen health,” said Kirkpatrick.

She also cautioned consumers to be mindful of any caffeine sensitivities they may have. However, the benefits of coffee have been seen in studies assessing both caffeinated and decaf options.

However, adding ingredients high in sugar or saturated fat could offset some of coffee’s potential health benefits.

Kirkpatrick noted that some studies suggest milk may enhance antioxidant activity. The current study did not examine whether coffee additions reduced its health benefits, but found that these ingredients contributed additional calories.

Other research has raised concerns about the potential health effects of consuming excessive added sugar and certain food additives.

“I suggest that my patients try to embrace a black cup of coffee as opposed to starting the day with sugar,” Kirkpatrick said.

She suggested that certain additions, such as chicory root or cinnamon, may enhance your brew while still providing benefits. Plain milk can also provide protein and calcium without added sugar.

“Starting the day with [something] sweet may make it difficult to limit sugary foods later in the day. Starting the day with a more bitter approach may [be] an important factor in keeping sugar down, as bitter compounds may positively impact appetite-regulating pathways,” said Kirkpatrick.
