#4809. Why We Might Give Tattooed Strangers a Little More Room

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Picture two people standing in line ahead of you. They look identical, except that one has visible tattoos. Would you find one more attractive? Would you feel equally comfortable standing close to both?

We know that physical appearance influences how we judge other people. But I wondered whether something as simple as a tattoo could also affect how comfortable we feel interacting with someone. To investigate this, I conducted a study, recently published in Evolutionary Psychological Science, involving 198 adults in the UK. Participants viewed two computer-generated figures, one male and one female, each shown with and without tattoos. The figures appeared at different distances, ranging from one metre to two-and-a-half metres. Participants rated how comfortable they would feel interacting with each figure at each distance, as well as how attractive they found them.

People generally felt slightly more comfortable with the non-tattooed figures than with their tattooed counterparts. The average comfort ratings were approximately 5.12 versus 4.95 on a seven-point scale. The difference was small but statistically significant, and it appeared for both male and female figures. I had expected tattoos to matter more when someone appeared closer. Surprisingly, they didn't. Although participants felt more comfortable as the distance increased, the effect of tattoos did not significantly change with distance. This suggests that tattoos may influence our general impression of someone rather than specifically making us uncomfortable when that person gets too close.

Here, the results depended on who was looking. Male participants rated both male and female figures as more attractive when they did not have tattoos. Female participants, however, showed no significant difference in attractiveness ratings between tattooed and non-tattooed figures. This is interesting because tattoos have sometimes been associated with masculinity, dominance, and risk-taking, characteristics that could potentially make someone more attractive. Yet women in this study did not find tattooed men more attractive than men without tattoos. In other words, the same physical feature can influence people's judgments differently, depending on the observer.

What I find particularly interesting is that participants knew nothing about the figures they were judging. They had no information about their personalities, backgrounds, or behaviour. Yet changing one visible feature was enough to influence their ratings. It is a small example of something much broader: how readily we form impressions of others based on appearance, often without knowing why.

This question has interested me for years and is also central to my recent book, Psychology of Attractiveness and Aesthetics: How We Perceive Beauty in People and Artwork, in which I explore how our visual experiences shape what we find attractive and aesthetically pleasing, from human faces and bodies to works of art.

The tattoo study adds another piece to that picture. Appearance does not simply influence what we find beautiful. It can also affect how comfortable we feel around other people. And perhaps the most interesting part is that our reactions to someone's appearance may tell us as much about ourselves as they do about the person we are judging. This is the first study to test tattoo effects on comfort distance ratings using controlled avatar stimuli and a behavioural-immune framework, suggesting tattoo-related interpersonal discomfort is driven more by affective, heuristic processes than deliberative disease-risk beliefs.

Pazhoohi, F. The Effect of Tattoos on Comfort Distance and Attractiveness Perceptions. Evolutionary Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40806-026-00506-1

#4808. Children made some of the Middle East’s oldest known clay figures

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 11, 2026 2:00 PM EST

About 10,000 years ago, a Neolithic culture in the southern Levant known as the Natufians became some of the first nomadic hunter-gatherers to transition towards agriculture. But even before this monumental lifestyle shift, members of the prehistoric community were already crafting symbolic figures from clay. What’s more, archaeologists say more than 150 recently discovered artifacts dating back 11,500 to 15,000 years ago are likely the earliest examples of their kind ever found in the Middle East. Their findings, published today in the journal PLOS One, suggest that even children sometimes had a role in creating these miniatures.

The Natufians lived in what is now known as the Fertile Crescent between 9,500 and 13,000 BCE. Pre-agrarian and semi-sedentary, the culture likely preceded the region’s first permanent Neolithic settlements. Although archaeologists previously located small figurines linked to the Natufians made from rocks and bones, these clay artifacts have larger implications. Crafting items from preexisting hard materials typically relies on intentionally shaping through processes like breaking, sanding, or whittling. The existence of clay items suggests that the Natufians didn’t just express themselves artistically and symbolically. They did so through materials that required additional steps like baking and hardening.

“This shift required diverse tools, skills, and knowledge, different from those needed for the manipulation of stone and bone,” the study’s authors wrote.

The figurines found at sites across present-day Israel include depictions of animals like birds and hooved mammals like deer, as well as both male and female individuals. Some of the pieces exhibit traces of pigment and other dyes, while others still feature ancient fingerprints of the artists themselves. Further examinations of these indentations shows that clay sculpting was an intergenerational craft, with both children and adults taking part in the activity.

“Thousands of years before agriculture and pottery emerged, people were already using clay to create figures, as part of their beliefs and knowledge of the natural world,” Laurent Davin, a study co-author and archaeologist at The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said in a statement. “What is particularly fascinating is the evidence that children were involved in making these objects, suggesting that creativity and cultural knowledge were shared across generations.”

BYD’s Flash Charging tech can charge an EV in as little as five minutes. Now, BYD is taking things a step further with integrated solar power and a robotic arm that plugs itself in. See how it all works in action.

After unveiling the Yangwang Altior in the UAE on Monday, its new ultra-luxury flagship electric sedan, BYD showcased its latest breakthrough technology.

The Chinese automaker launched a new integrated charging system in the Abu Dhabi desert that brings BYD’s “Three Green Dreams” to life.

In 2006, BYD president and CEO Wang Chuanfu revealed his vision of “Three Green Dreams,” including harnessing solar power to generate renewable energy, storing that energy in batteries, and replacing gas-powered vehicles with electric ones that run on clean energy.

The new charging system is the “world’s first,” according to BYD, to integrate solar power generation, energy storage, Flash Charging, and robotic charging together in one solution.

BYD’s Flash Charging tech enables a vehicle’s battery to charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes, essentially the same time it takes to fill up at a gas station. For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.

The new robotic charging arm automatically locates the vehicle’s charging port, opens its cover, plugs in, and then removes it once the session is over.

By combining robotic charging with its Automated Valet Parking, BYD said the new tech goes beyond automated driving and parking to the charging process itself.

Once the vehicle is parked, the robotic charging arm automatically takes over and connects it to Flash Charging without the driver even touching the cable.

A post shared by Michael Martinez (@mmichael_martinez)

Michaël Martinez, head of marketing at BYD France, posted a video (shown above) showcasing the new charging tech in action.

The integrated solution is built around BYD’s Solar-Storage-Charging (SSC) system, fusing solar energy generation, battery storage, and its 5-minute Flash Charging tech. Together, the setup captures energy from the sun, stores it, and distributes it as needed.

The new technology is part of BYD’s wider Flash Charging rollout. By the end of 2027, the company plans to deploy 6,000 Flash Charging stations globally.

New EV prices edged up in October, but buyers still paid less than they did a year ago. The average transaction price for a new EV in the US was $56,220, up 1% from September and down 2.7% from October 2025, according to Kelley Blue Book, a Cox Automotive brand.

Across all new vehicles, the average hit a record $51,109, up 1.3% from September and 2.1% year over year, even as prices rose more slowly than they typically do in October.

#4804. Weight Gain During Long-Term Antipsychotic Use

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Most antipsychotics cause some degree of weight gain. They are generally classified into three categories according to the degree of weight gain each causes. Weight gain caused by antipsychotics can be a deterrent to using them, or a motivation to go off antipsychotics prematurely. For someone like me who has been on antipsychotics for 26 years, I have experienced a lifetime of managing weight fluctuation, gaining a good deal of weight and then losing it a few times. Here is an account of my journey of weight gain and loss while taking antipsychotics and what I have gleaned from these experiences.

My first antipsychotic was Zyprexa, which I first started taking in 2001. I was not informed by my psychiatrist at that time that this drug causes weight gain, and I was on a higher dose. Accordingly, I had no idea I was taking the antipsychotic notorious for causing the most weight gain, and the psychiatrist never shared with me the fact that the medicine could be a factor in my weight gain.

I was already so hard on myself for taking an antipsychotic in the first place, and the weight gain, which I blamed on myself, was another source of shame. I couldn’t understand why I was gaining weight when nothing had changed with how much I eat and how much I was exercising, so I felt like my life was out of control in multiple ways. It felt similar to having some sort of mental illness but not really understanding what I was up against or what I could do about it.

It’s so easy to be hard on yourself about weight gain, and it’s also so incredibly hard to properly attribute your medicine for causing it. Because of stigma, we are taught that mental illness should be under our control, just like society tells us that weight gain is really always under our control as well. Taking an antipsychotic can tug at your self-esteem, and weight gain just intensifies any tendency for low self-esteem and self-blame.

I was on Abilify and experienced almost no weight gain with it, so I was happy. However, I suddenly started having involuntary tongue movements with this drug after it had worked well for me for years, so I had no choice but to go back on Zyprexa, just a month or two before I started trying on wedding dresses after my engagement. As someone who was anorexic in college and still body dysmorphic, gaining a bunch of weight right before trying on wedding dresses, when most people try to be their thinnest, seemed so unfair. I took it as a sign that I would never be able to move on with my life.

I was thankful that my psychiatrist put me on a high dose of Metformin to help manage weight gain caused by Zyprexa. The Metformin felt to me like validation and acknowledgement that, yes, it’s not all my fault if I gain weight on this drug and that there are real, demonstrated ways that psychiatry acknowledges and helps us with this issue. Even with Metformin, I put on 15 pounds, but I successfully worked hard to lose it all before it was time for dress alterations. But it did feel like an unnecessary hurdle and annoying complication, a reminder that my illness is never over.

I’ve gained and lost so many pounds through antipsychotic use. The weight creeps in until one day I’m forced to address it, then I go through an organized effort to lose it. Growing up, I was a competitive athlete who thought weighing 140 pounds was a lot, but for most of my adult life on antipsychotics, weighing 140 is no longer achievable, or if so, unsustainable.

I’m convinced the reason I gained over 60 pounds while pregnant with my child was due to being on Zyprexa at the time. However, I did lose the weight through walking, calorie reduction, and nursing. With the help of Metformin, I did not get gestational diabetes. I’m now on Quetiapine, and it is supposed to be a moderate weight gainer, but I don’t think I have much of an easier time keeping weight off with this drug than with Zyprexa. However, since Quetiapine is perfect for avoiding a terrible side effect I get with every other drug, there is no way I will ever take any other drug again. This time, when weight loss was called for at age 47, I needed to go on a GLP to lose it.

One thing I can say about this 26-year journey of weight gain and dieting since I've been on antipsychotics is that I am healthier for it and make healthier choices. Because I have less control over my metabolism, I have made other critical health choices that will pay off in the long run in multiple ways. Giving up gluten is a big deal for me, especially with thyroid diseases, as well as giving up almost all soda and alcohol. I’ve also been a vegetarian for 20 years, for a number of reasons in addition to health. Some of these choices started as ways I could mitigate weight gain caused by antipsychotics, but they turned out to have benefited me in other very real ways.

Another huge shift for me is caring more about my health than fixating on the number on the scale. I’m no longer concerned with going back to 140—I’m more interested in longevity and keeping up with my 7-year-old son. Through my cycle of weight gain and loss, I’ve given up on the idea that success is a clothing size; it’s about my bloodwork all looking good, reducing inflammation, feeling energetic, and exercising regularly.

One of the toughest aspects of serious mental illness is the elusiveness. You can’t visualize it; there is no blood test, and you may get re-diagnosed by different doctors. Sometimes there is no clear answer on what to do at all. You can’t control what effects antipsychotics have on you, and sometimes discerning what is under your control and what is being dictated by the antipsychotic is difficult. Weight gain caused by antipsychotics can feel the same way, leaving you feeling powerless and frustrated.

It’s hard and seems unfair that making the right and responsible choice for your mental health can have other health consequences. But staying on antipsychotics, even if they cause weight gain, has been critical for my full remission from schizophrenia for 15 years and for becoming a wife and mother. Unpredictable weight gain has also led me to make important health decisions for myself when it comes to food and drink that will benefit me for the rest of my life. I’ve also made other good health choices that I probably would not have made if I did not have a tendency to gain weight due to antipsychotics. I’ve also learned to lean on internal means of validation and self-esteem instead of superficial, external means.

#4803. A wobbly exoplanet vanished—but astronomers aren’t worried

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 11, 2026 4:01 PM EST

For the first time, astronomers witnessed a gigantic exoplanet dramatically vanish from view. But the “hot Jupiter” located about 1,000 light-years from Earth didn’t evaporate into the vacuum of space. Instead, the gravitational pull from an uncomfortably close neighbor is causing TOI-2535 b to wobble in its orbit thanks to the same dynamics dictating solar and lunar eclipses. The unusual discovery is detailed in a study recently published in Astrophysical Journal Letters, and relies on observations gathered by NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) orbital telescope.

“We think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular, but that’s not true,” Samuel Yee, a University of California Los Angeles (UCLA) astronomer and study co-author, explained in a recent profile. “If there are multiple planets in a system, they can affect each other’s orbits.”

Astronomers first began examining TOI-2535 b in April 2019 using TESS. The eagle-eyed telescope identifies new planets by flagging subtle changes in stellar brightness. These changes are often caused by a previously unknown planet’s transit in front of its star as seen from Earth. In some ways, TOI-2535 b resembles our solar system’s largest planet, but it is even closer to its own star than Mercury is to our sun. While Mercury takes 88 days to complete the trip, TOI-2535 b circles back around once every 8.25 days.

While using TESS to get glimpses of TOI-2535 b over the next seven years, researchers realized the hot Jupiter’s transits didn’t occur on a regular schedule like most other planets. Instead, the exoplanet’s light fluctuations could arrive upwards of six hours earlier or later than predicted. Over time, astronomers also noticed these transits become shallower and shorter. Then, in March, TOI-2535 b simply didn’t show up during the space telescope’s scan of the system.

Researchers including Yee now believe their hot Jupiter isn’t alone—it actually has an incredibly close gas giant neighbor with a comparatively tilted orbit. The two planets’ relationship causes them to essentially wobble like a pair of tops, eventually throwing one another out of alignment so that they disappear from Earth’s viewpoint.

“This is the most extreme example we’ve seen because the two planets are interacting so strongly,” said Yee. “The planet’s orbit is tilting so quickly that its transit disappeared while we were watching.”

The forces at play are the same as those that ensure eclipses don’t follow a regularly repeating cycle. UCLA astrophysicist and study co-author Erik Petigura explained that this is due to the moon’s tilted orbit, which comes from its cataclysmic early formation following a collision with Earth.

“If the moon’s orbit around the Earth was perfectly aligned with the Earth’s orbit around the sun, we would see an eclipse every month,” Petigura explained.

Yee, Petigura, and their colleagues are lucky to have spotted TOI-2535’s disappearing act when they did. Based on their calculations, its next transit in front of its star won’t occur for another 30 to 50 years—although they may see its partner planet sooner once it emerges from behind its stellar anchor.

#4802. Lucid CEO admits it ‘did not even know where cars were’ and lost orders

Lucid (LCID) CEO Silvio Napoli admitted on the company’s Q3 earnings call that, as recently as this summer, the automaker “did not even know where cars were.” Buyers placed orders, Lucid took up to two weeks to locate and deliver a car, and some of those buyers walked away.

That’s a rough admission from a company sitting on thousands of unsold vehicles. And it’s a problem Tesla ran into, and fixed, back in 2018 at more than ten times Lucid’s current volume.

Napoli made the comment when an analyst asked whether Lucid’s deliveries would go up or down in the fourth quarter. He said that at the start of Q3, the company had orders where it “would take sometimes two weeks to deliver to the customer, and so we would lose the order.”

He said Lucid now has visibility on which cars are being built, where they’re shipped, where they’re stored, and when they can reach a customer. A new commercial team also now sells the cars it knows are available on the day a customer wants one.

Lucid built 3,228 more vehicles than it delivered in the first half of 2026, including 5,500 built but only 3,093 delivered in Q1. Its inventory hit $1.38 billion on the balance sheet at the end of June, which is why we reported earlier this year that Lucid had to adjust production after a bloated Q1 inventory.

So Lucid had thousands of cars on lots and in transit, and it was still losing buyers because it couldn’t match a car to an order fast enough.

In Q3, Lucid cut production to 2,954 vehicles and delivered 3,806, down 7% year over year. Finished goods inventory fell by almost 15% during the quarter, according to new CFO Alexander De Bock. Inventory stood at $1.22 billion on September 30.

Tesla learned this lesson the hard way during the Model 3 ramp.

By Q3 2018, Tesla was making roughly 4,000 Model 3s per week. That’s more cars every week than Lucid delivers in a full quarter today. Deliveries tripled or quadrupled in some markets, and the bottleneck moved from the factory to the trucks.

Elon Musk tweeted in September 2018 that Tesla had “gone from production hell to delivery logistics hell.” A week later, he said Tesla was facing an “extreme shortage of car carrier trailers” and had started building its own car carriers to keep cars moving. Tesla also launched door-to-door delivery and asked existing owners to help at delivery centers.

It didn’t stop there. In November 2018, with the federal tax credit about to be cut in half for Tesla buyers, Musk said Tesla had bought trucking companies and locked in contracts with major haulers. Tesla moved cars east by truck instead of rail to cut weeks off transit times.

Tesla delivered 83,500 vehicles in Q3 2018, including 55,840 Model 3s, a record at the time.

When Model 3 reached Europe in February 2019, the first ship docked at Zeebrugge in Belgium and Tesla immediately had trouble processing the cars at the port.

About a week after the first ship arrived, Tesla ended its contract with the company preparing Model 3s at the port and took over the work itself. The target was 3,000 cars per week coming through one port.

It worked. By March 2019, Tesla delivered more than 5,300 Model 3s in Norway alone, making it the best-selling car in the country by a wide margin. A car that’s sitting at a port or on a lot doesn’t make anyone money. Tesla treated delivery speed as a sales tool, not a back-office job.

We later learned from Musk himself that this “logistic hell” was almost the nail in Tesla’s coffin. The CEO said that Tesla was at the brink of bankruptcy at the time.

I like to think people were relatively patient with Tesla's growing pains when Model 3 was ramping up in 2018, largely because there weren't many alternatives for a sporty, relatively affordable EV.

But it's 2026. Buyers have plenty of options now, and the patience that early EV adopters once had for these kinds of mistakes is long gone.

This is one of the most embarrassing admissions we’ve heard on an earnings call, and credit to Napoli for saying it out loud. Most executives would have blamed “demand” and moved on.

But it explains a lot. Lucid’s problem has never been the cars. The Air and Gravity are excellent products. The problem has been everything around them: service, software, and now we learn, basic inventory tracking. When you’re spending about $273,000 for every car you deliver, losing a buyer because you can’t find their car two weeks after they ordered is brutal.

Tesla solved this at 4,000 Model 3s a week while fighting for its own survival. Lucid is moving fewer than 300 cars a week. This isn’t a hard problem at that scale. It’s a discipline problem, and Napoli is right to call it that.

#4801. GLP-1s May Help Lower Diabetes, Heart Risks Better Than Standard Prevention

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

GLP-1 drugs are more effective in helping prevent type 2 diabetes than the commonly prescribed medication metformin, according to a new study.

Researchers said GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro were more likely to reduce blood sugar to healthy levels in people with prediabetes and obesity.

They added that people prescribed GLP-1 medications had a lower risk of progressing from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

The researchers noted that GLP-1 users also had a lower risk of death from any cause as well as fewer heart attacks, strokes, and heart failure events compared with metformin users.

“The great news with prediabetes is that it’s still possible to reverse the progression of the disease,” said Vinicius de Sousa Barzon Serra, MD, a study author and research fellow in cardiovascular medicine at the Mayo Clinic in Scottsdale, Arizona, in a press release. “This research may add to the case for considering GLP-1 medications earlier for certain patients, rather than waiting until they develop type 2 diabetes.”

Serra noted that metformin still remains an effective treatment for people with prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.

“This is less about replacing one medication with another and more about discussing additional options with specific patients,” he said.

The researchers presented their findings at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago. The research has not been published yet in a peer-reviewed journal.

David Cutler, MD, a family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, wasn’t involved in the study, but said the findings were “quite impressive.”

“It elevates the comfort of prescribing GLP-1 drugs as a front-line treatment,” he told Healthline.

Robert Eckel, MD, a former president of the American Heart Association who was likewise not involved in the study, agrees the research provides more options for patients and prescribers.

“GLP-1s provide another option for prevention, perhaps as an add-on therapy. However, costs and access to these medications are important factors,” said Eckel, an endocrinologist at the University of Colorado School of Medicine, in the press release.

For their study, the researchers analyzed the medical records of 256,000 adults in the United States with prediabetes and obesity. About 76% of the subjects were women, and the average age of the participants was 52.

About half of those studied were taking GLP-1 drugs with the active ingredient semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, or dulaglutide.

The other half had been prescribed metformin, a medication used to help manage blood sugar levels in adults and some children with type 2 diabetes by decreasing glucose production in the liver, reducing glucose absorption from food, and improving the body’s insulin sensitivity.

The researchers reported that the people in the study who were taking GLP-1 drugs had a 1.5 times higher chance of reversing high blood sugar to healthy levels compared to people who were using metformin.

The researchers also noted that GLP-1 medication users had a 31% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes and a 41% lower risk of death from any cause.

They added that GLP-1 medications were associated with 15% fewer heart attacks, 20% fewer strokes, 25% fewer cases of heart failure, and 8% fewer cases of atrial fibrillation (AFib), a common type of irregular heartbeat.

The researchers cautioned that their study is observational and, therefore, cannot prove a cause-and-effect relationship. They also noted they relied on prescription records, so the frequency and dosage at which patients took their medication was not reflected.

In addition, the GLP-1 drugs were grouped together, so individual differences between medications were not considered.

Eckel said in the news release that the benefits for people taking GLP-1 drugs were probably mainly due to weight loss. Eckel noted that the research results open up a wide range of possibilities.

“This is an important finding because the GLP-1 receptor agonists are commonly used today and this is a population that in the transition from prediabetes to diabetes are at increasing risk for cardiovascular disease,” Eckel said in a taped interview alongside the study findings.

Cutler pointed out that several GLP-1 drugs also target blood sugar levels and insulin production. They could be effective in people with prediabetes who don’t have weight management issues.

Cutler noted that these people, however, might be reluctant to take GLP-1 drugs because they may not be experiencing symptoms of their prediabetes but could develop side effects with the medications.

“They would not be getting any immediate benefits,” Cutler said. He added that metformin, which was first used clinically in 1958, remains an effective alternative. “It’s been proven safe, effective, and it’s very cheap,” Cutler said.

It’s estimated that 40 million people in the United States have diabetes, with more than 90% of those cases being type 2 diabetes, a chronic condition characterized by high blood glucose levels that results from the body’s ineffective response to insulin or insufficient insulin production.

It’s also estimated that 115 million adults in the United States have prediabetes, a condition in which a person has higher-than-normal blood sugar levels but not high enough to be diagnosed as type 2 diabetes.

Around 5–10% of people with prediabetes develop diabetes every year. More broadly, up to 70% of people with prediabetes eventually develop diabetes.

Medication is sometimes prescribed for people with type 2 diabetes and prediabetes. Lifestyle changes can help reverse type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, as well as prevent the progression from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

Cutler said the lifestyle changes needed to prevent type 2 diabetes are pretty clear.

“The most important thing for people with prediabetes to know is they should lose weight, reduce their carbs, exercise daily and, if that doesn’t work, then consider medication,” he said.

#4800. Kia launches two new PV5 electric van variants in the UK

Kia opened orders for two new PV5 electric van variants, the PV5 Chassis and PV5 Cargo L2/H2, in the UK.

The PV5 is Kia’s first fully electric van from its Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) business. Built on Hyundai Motor’s dedicated modular skateboard platform, E-GMP.S, Kia can easily swap body styles to enable “limitless possibilities.”

So far, the PV5 has mostly been available in Passenger and Cargo body styles with several different variations.

Kia added the PV5 Chassis, an open-bed model that can be converted into just about anything. In the UK, Kia is offering conversions through TGS Automotive Group, including lightweight tipper, Dropside, and Box solutions.

The PV5 Chassis is available exclusively with the long-range 71.2 kWh battery in the UK, which Kia said could offer a potential WLTP range of up to 258 miles (416 km).

For reference, the PV5 Cargo L2/H1, which uses the same 71.2 kWh battery, offers a WLTP range of up to 258 miles (416 km). Other markets will also have a standard-range 51.1 kWh option.

The Chassis model is 4,610 mm long, 1,895 mm wide, and 1,935 mm tall, with a 2,995 mm wheelbase.

Its compact size and 5.5-meter turning radius, Kia said, make it easy to maneuver in city streets, construction sites, and other tight work areas.

Inside, the PV5 Chassis features two seats. Like other variants, it includes a 12.9″ navigation screen and a 7.5″ driver display with standard wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

The Chassis model supports DC fast charging up to 120 kW, enabling the battery to charge from 10% to 80% in about 30 minutes. Using an 11 kW AC supply, it takes about 6 hours and 30 minutes to charge from 10% to 100%.

Payload depends on the configuration. Kia said the Dropside offers a payload of up to 633 kg, while the Tipper can carry 561 kg.

In the UK, the PV5 Chassis is now on sale from £32,916 ($43,400) on the road, including the expected £5,000 ($6,700) UK Zero Emission Van Grant.

However, it’s an “incomplete vehicle,” as Kia describes it. The converted PV5 Dropside is priced from £40,110 ($53,500) on the road, including the ZEVG, while the PV5 Tipper starts at £41,310 ($55,000).

Kia also launched the larger PV5 Cargo L2/H2 in the UK. The new variant is 4,695mm long, 1,895mm wide, and 2,200mm high, with a 2,995mm wheelbase.

The taller roof opens up an internal cargo-area height of 1,815mm. It also offers a greater load capacity than the L1/H1 and L2/H2, with 5.2 cubic meters.

It’s available in three- and four-door configurations with the choice of two or three seats. The three-door versions have a maximum payload of 630 kg, while the four-door models have dual sliding doors and offer a payload of up to 600 kg. Both versions can tow up to 1,500 kg.

Like the Chassis model, the PV5 Cargo L2/H2 is available in the UK exclusively with the 71.2 kWh battery, which provides a WLTP range of up to 239 miles.

Inside, it features the same setup as the other PV5 variants, including a 12.9″ touchscreen navigation screen and a 7.5″ driver display.

The base PV5 Cargo L2/H2 Essential two-seat starts at £35,016 ($46,700), on the road, including ZEVG.

#4799. How to Not Lose Your Cool This Holiday Season

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

While the holidays can bring a great deal of joy, they can also trigger anger in a lot of people. Think having to face difficult people during annual social gatherings, being stuck in traffic or stranded at an airport because of delays, or feeling underappreciated for all the effort you’ve put into a holiday that others may not have acknowledged.

Anger is a powerful emotion. Chronically angry people are more likely to suffer from heart disease, diabetes, and impaired immune functioning. They're also more likely to have unhappy marriages, be lonelier, and struggle at work.

Anger itself is not the problem. It's a normal and healthy emotion like any other. But when it goes unchecked, it can make us do and say things that cause irreparable damage or act in ways we deeply regret.

To help you keep your cool this holiday season, here are five anger-management techniques you can start using—today.

Look around your surrounding environment and try to find five things that are blue. Alternatively, you can seek out five things that begin with the letter A. Either approach helps shift your attention from the source of anger to a neutral stimulus. This brief break helps you de-escalate through cognitive shifting by allowing your emotions to cool down. The more time we spend ruminating and focusing on what’s upsetting us, the more hotheaded we can become. Distraction techniques like these interrupt that anger-rumination-explosion cycle, reducing activity in the amygdala and allowing our heart rates and blood pressure to come back to baseline.

Inhale all the way. Hold your breath for three to four seconds. Exhale all the way (try to make your exhale longer than your inhale). Hold your breath again at the bottom of that exhale for another three to four seconds. Repeat several times until you feel a reduction in distress. This breathwork technique and others like it help regulate the nervous system by increasing activity within the parasympathetic nervous system—the branch of the autonomic nervous system undergirding resting and digesting functions—and downshifting activity within the sympathetic (fight/flight) nervous system.

When you feel yourself getting heated, try to imagine the anger you’re feeling as an object in your body. First, where is it? Then, what does it look like? Feel like? What’s its temperature and texture; its weight? Be as descriptive as you can. Then, take a deep breath in and, with that breath, imagine creating space around the object in your body. On the exhale, imagine breathing out its intensity—almost like you’re cooling off the object of anger in your body.

Many studies have found that mindfulness techniques such as this help to ease anger, in part by creating some distance between you and the anger itself, so that anger doesn’t take you on as great a roller coaster ride. Taking time to visualize and work with the emotion in the body also helps slow you down, so you don’t knee-jerked-ly blurt out something nasty or otherwise act impulsively in a way that may haunt you (and possibly ruin Thanksgiving dinner).

If you feel yourself starting to get worked up—you're gritting your teeth, your face is flushed, your breathing is shallow, your fists are clenched—see if you can excuse yourself to splash some very cold water on your face or hold some ice cubes to your chest or your temples. If you’re in a part of the world where it’s cold during the holiday season, go take a walk outside in the icy air. Exposure to very cold temperatures helps to trigger the diving reflex, which quickly lowers heart rate and can essentially shock your body back into a less elevated state.

This one is especially helpful for dealing with difficult people over the holidays. If you’re surrounded by folks who aren’t aligned with you politically, can be quite rude, or make unnecessary comments about your life, body, or any other personal aspect, imagine a force field around you. Really go deep with the visualization here. What color is the force field? What is it made of—ice? Fire? Laser beams? Does it make a noise? Then, imagine the difficult person’s (or persons’) statements bouncing off of the force field (better yet, if they make a funny noise when they do so), leaving you safe and protected. You can go the extra mile and imagine the statements bouncing back and tripping the other person, spilling all over them, or whatever other amusing visual will bring you more of a smile than a grimace.

All of these techniques can be useful in moments of high frustration leading to intense anger. (I use them with my clients, and also with myself.) If you find yourself becoming angry quite often or if you find it particularly challenging to de-escalate and not do things you later feel badly about, it may be worth connecting with a therapist who can help you practice skills like these as well as do some deeper work around the origins of any chronic anger you may be struggling with. Don’t hesitate to get help if this is the case. Your heart health will thank you if you do.
